claims.text: Vacuum heat treatment at approximately 500 °C improves the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings during sliding at 500–700 °C.
The approximately 500 °C heat treatment refines the coating's near-surface microstructure.
The heat treatment stabilizes grain boundaries and promotes nanostructural features.
The intervention promotes formation of a thin, adherent, protective oxide layer.
The heat-treated coating has greater hardness than the as-deposited coating.
Higher microhardness contributes to improved wear resistance after 500 °C vacuum heat treatment.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu baseline has coarser grains and unmodified grain-boundary chemistry relative to the treated coating.
The treated surface contains refined grains, nanotwins, and high dislocation densities.
Stabilized grain boundaries limit excessive plastic flow and intergranular weakening during high-temperature sliding.
The protective oxide layer reduces metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
The combined microstructural and oxide-layer effects reduce both adhesive and abrasive wear.
The heat-treated coating will have a lower wear rate than the as-deposited coating under otherwise identical high-temperature, high-load conditions.
The heat-treated coating will show less grain-boundary oxidation and spallation than the as-deposited coating.
The proposed mechanism dominates at approximately 500–700 °C under high normal loads.
At temperatures substantially outside 500–700 °C or under different wear modes, other wear mechanisms may dominate.
The specified high normal loads are representative of industrial protective-coating applications.
